title: OPPOSITION: WETLOOK (003193135)
text:
OPPOSITION Nо B 3 193 135

Mrkk Aps, Stokagervej 5, 8240 Risskov, Denmark (opponent), represented by Otello Law Firm, Sommervej 31F, 3. tv, 8210 Aarhus V, Denmark (professional representative) 

a g a i n s t

Deluxe Holding Aps, Kobbervej 7, 6000 Kolding, Denmark (applicant), represented by Løje Ip, Øster Alle 42, 6. Floor, 2100 Copenhagen Ø, Denmark (professional representative). 

On 30/07/2026, the Opposition Division takes the following

DECISION:

REASONS

On 05/04/2023, the opponent filed an opposition against all the goods of European Union trade mark application No 18 843 761 ‘WETLOOK’ (word mark). The opposition is based non-registered trade mark ‘WETLOOK’ and other sign ‘WETLOOK’, purportedly used in the course of trade in Denmark. The opponent invoked Article 8(4) EUTMR.

PRELIMINARY REMARK

The contested sign was partially refused registration in Examination Decision of 06/02/2025, namely for all the contested goods in Class 11. This decision was fully upheld in decision of the Board of Appeal of 22/10/2025, in case R 496/2025-5. 

Therefore, the present opposition is considered to be directed against the remaining contested goods, namely all the goods in Class 4. 

Furthermore, while the opponent in the notice of opposition invoked other sign ‘WETLOOK’ used in the course of trade in Denmark, it is recalled that this category consists of signs that are not registered and used as trade marks and of a great number of different earlier rights, such as rights to a company name, a trade name, and titles of protected literary/artistic works or the right to a sign under passing off. Since in the present case the opponent failed to indicate the kind and nature of this earlier right, which is an absolute requirement, and which serves to determine the scope of the opposition and the applicant’s defence depends on it (see, to this extent, 28/06/2023, T-452/22 , Hofmag / Hofmag, EU:T:2023:362, § 59-61), the said earlier right cannot be taken into account and the opposition must be deemed to be inadmissible as regards the opponent’s other sign used in the course of trade, 

The opposition will proceed as far as it is based non-registered trade mark ‘WETLOOK’ used in the course of trade of more than mere local significance in Denmark. 

NON-REGISTERED MARK USED IN THE COURSE OF TRADE — ARTICLE 8(4) EUTMR

The opposition is based on non-registered trade mark ‘WETLOOK’ purportedly used in the course of trade in Denmark in relation to illuminating wax; illuminants; candles and wicks for lighting; candles for lighting; lighting apparatus and installations; LED candles. 

According to Article 8(4) EUTMR, upon opposition by the proprietor of a non-registered trade mark or of another sign used in the course of trade of more than mere local significance, the trade mark applied for will not be registered where and to the extent that, pursuant to the Union legislation or the law of the Member State governing that sign:

(a) rights to that sign were acquired prior to the date of application for registration of the European Union trade mark, or the date of the priority claimed for the application for registration of the European Union trade mark;

(b) that sign confers on its proprietor the right to prohibit the use of a subsequent trade mark.

Therefore, the grounds of refusal of Article 8(4) EUTMR are subject to the following requirements:

	the earlier sign must have been used in the course of trade of more than local significance prior to the filing of the contested trade mark;

	pursuant to the law governing it, prior to the filing of the contested trade mark, the opponent acquired rights to the sign on which the opposition is based, including the right to prohibit the use of a subsequent trade mark;

	the conditions under which the use of a subsequent trade mark may be prohibited are fulfilled in respect of the contested trade mark.

These conditions are cumulative. Therefore, where a sign does not satisfy one of those conditions, the opposition based on a non-registered trade mark or other signs used in the course of trade within the meaning of Article 8(4) EUTMR cannot succeed.

a) Prior use in the course of trade of more than mere local significance

The condition requiring use in the course of trade is a fundamental requirement, without which the sign in question cannot enjoy any protection against the registration of a European Union trade mark, irrespective of the requirements to be met under national law in order to acquire exclusive rights. Furthermore, such use must indicate that the sign in question is of more than mere local significance.

It must be recalled that the object of the condition laid down in Article 8(4) EUTMR relating to use in the course of trade of a sign of more than mere local significance is to limit conflicts between signs by precluding an earlier right that is not sufficiently definite — that is to say, important and significant in the course of trade — from preventing registration of a new European Union trade mark. A right of opposition of that kind must be reserved for signs with a real and actual presence on their relevant market. To be capable of preventing registration of a new sign, the sign relied on in opposition must actually be used in a sufficiently significant manner in the course of trade, and its geographical extent must not be merely local, which implies, where the territory in which that sign is protected may be regarded as other than local, that the sign must be used in a substantial part of that territory. In order to ascertain whether that is the case, account must be taken of the duration and intensity of the use of the sign as a distinctive element for its addressees, namely purchasers and consumers as well as suppliers and competitors. In that regard, the use made of the sign in advertising and commercial correspondence is of particular relevance. In addition, the condition relating to use in the course of trade must be assessed separately for each of the territories in which the right relied on in support of the opposition is protected. Finally, use of the sign in the course of trade must be shown to have occurred before the date of the application for registration of the European Union trade mark (29/03/2011, C-96/09 P, BUD / BUD, EU:C:2011:189, § 157, 159-160, 163, 166).

Therefore, the fact that a sign confers on its proprietor an exclusive right throughout the national territory is in itself insufficient to prove that it is of more than mere local significance within the meaning of Article 8(4) EUTMR. The requirement of ‘more than local significance’ relates also to the use that is made of the sign on the basis of which the opposition is entered, and not only to the geographic area in which the sign may be protected according to the law governing the sign in question (29/03/2011, C-96/09 P, BUD / BUD, EU:C:2011:189, § 156).

In the present case, the contested trade mark was filed on 03/03/2023. Therefore, the opponent was required to prove that the sign on which the opposition is based was used in the course of trade of more than local significance in Denmark. The evidence must also show that the opponent’s sign has been used in the course of trade for non-registered sign ‘Wetlook’ 

On 29/02/2024, the opponent filed the following evidence: 

Appendix 12: The provision from the Danish Trademark Act and the ruling from the Danish

Supreme Court in 2000 (U 2000.1351 H), translated into English. These documents are intended to show that in Denmark it is possible to obtain an unregistered trade mark as soon as you use the mark, and that the requirements for establishing such a right are very low, as long as the communication of the mark is directed at the public, and not just internally. 

Specifically, the opponent highlighted the following part of the relevant Danish law: 

The Danish Court ruling also concluded, according to the translation provided by the opponent, that a trade mark right can be established also through commencement of use of a trademark within the country. 

Appendix 13: a printout from Punktum.dk (the administrator for .dk-domain names), showing that lyshygge.dk was registered by the opponent on 7 July 2015.

Appendix 14: a printout from the video on Youtube.com of lyshygge.dk (the opponent) concerning “Luca Wetlook”.

Translation of the description of the video, originally in Danish, was provided by the opponent as follows: 

“Luca Wetlook has landed! 

As something brand new, we can now present our newest collection – Luca Wetlook. The collection has a characteristic “wetlook’ on the top of the pillar candle, which looks like melted candle wax. It given an even more realistic expression”. 

The video has more than 144.000 views.

Appendix 15: printouts from Facebook and Instagram, dated 25/08/2021, showing that the opponent launched the “Luca Wetlook” candle on these social platforms. 

Facebook launch page, with 680 views.

Instagram launch page, with 329 views.

Appendix 16: examples from the opponent’s Dutch Facebook page and online retailers of the opponent’s, to show that since their launch, the opponent has sold electric candles with shiny surface as “Luca Wetlook” or marketed these with the product description “wetlook”. 

The above screenshot is taken from led-nordic.nl, dated 01/01/2023, and is in Dutch. The products in the photos do not bear the sign invoked. 

Assessment of the evidence

General considerations

The requirements of use of the sign in the course of trade and of more than mere local significance, are apparent from the very wording of Article 8(4) EUTMR and must therefore be interpreted in the light of European Union law. The EUTMR sets out uniform standards, relating to the use of signs and their significance, which are consistent with the principles underlying the system established by that regulation (14/05/2013, T-321/11 & T-322/11, Parte della libertà, EU:T:2013:240, § 31; 23/10/2013, T-581/11, baby Bambolina, EU:T:2013:553, § 23). It must be examined independently of the requirements of the relevant national law for the acquisition of a company sign. The mere fact that a sign confers on its proprietor an exclusive right throughout the national territory is not in itself sufficient to prove that it is of more than mere local significance within the meaning of the fourth sentence of Article 8 of the EUTMR (24/03/2009, T-318/06 – T-321/06, General Optica, EU:T:2009:77, § 39; 19/11/2014, T-344/13, FUNNY BANDS, EU:T:2014:974, § 24). 

The significance of a sign used to identify specific business activities must be determined in relation to its identification function. Account must be taken of the geographical area in which it is used to identify the proprietor’s economic activity, as well as the economic significance of the sign, which must be assessed in relation to the duration, the intensity of its use, the group of addressees and the exposure given to the sign, for example in advertising and on the internet (24/03/2009, T-318/06 – T-321/06, General Optica, EU:T:2009:77, § 37). 

Furthermore, when assessing use of the signs of more than mere local significance, it must be borne in mind that this cannot be proved by means of probabilities or suppositions, but must be demonstrated by solid and objective evidence of effective and sufficient use of the sign on the market (23/10/2013, T-581/11, Baby Bambolina).

On the basis of the above, the criterion of ‘more than mere local significance’ requires more than just a geographical examination. The economic impact of the use of the sign must also be evaluated. Consideration must be given, and the evidence must relate, to these elements:

a)	the intensity of use (i.e. sales made under the sign);

b)	the length of use;

c)	the spread of the goods (i.e. the locations of the customers);

d)	the advertising under the sign and the media used for that advertising, including the distribution of the advertising.

The evidence filed by the opponent

The opponent filed excerpts from the relevant Danish law, and from a Danish Court decision. However, the Opposition Division considers that these excerpts in themselves do not serve to prove that the opponent’s mark has been used in more than local significance. These documents provide a general overview and merely state that starting to use a trade mark establishes a right to that mark. However, they do not concern the requirement of more than local significance including that of continuous use. Contrary to what the opponent submits, the fact that a sign confers on its proprietor an exclusive right throughout the national territory is in itself insufficient to prove that it is of more than mere local significance within the meaning of Article 8(4) EUTMR. The requirement of ‘more than local significance’ relates also to the use that is made of the sign on the basis of which the opposition is entered, and not only to the geographic area in which the sign may be protected according to the law governing the sign in question (29/03/2011, C-96/09 P, BUD / BUD, EU:C:2011:189, § 156).

The additional documents filed, namely screenshots from the opponent’s social platform pages merely provide information that the opponent published certain information in relation to its ‘wetlook’ candles. Also, the number of views of these pages, except those on Youtube page, are rather low, and they merely give a static view of the opponent’s product. However, the evidence fails completely to provide any further information as regards the continuous use of the mark in relation to the goods or the actual geographical scope thereof. The remaining evidence, namely a screenshot from a Dutch webpage bears no relevance to the opponent’s mark in the Danish market. 

Furthermore, screenshots of social medial platform pages cannot serve to prove any actual extent of use of the mark in question. The mere fact that ‘wetlook’ candles were offered for sale at a given moment does not mean that they were also actually sold in Denmark. 

The onus is on the opponent to submit evidence that demonstrates that there has been use, in a more than mere local context, for the business activities invoked. While the opponent is not obliged to reveal sensitive business information, it should nevertheless be able to provide those items that show beyond doubt use of the earlier signs in the relevant territories. It is recalled that whether or not a trade sign is of more than mere local significance may be established, for example, by producing invoices issued to clients of a significant part of the relevant territory, or press cuttings showing the degree of recognition on the part of the public of the sign relied on. Also, the opponent could have used additional means of proving its case, for example by providing price lists, affidavit, turnover and sales figures or marketing expenditures, to name but a few.  

In the present case, the evidence fails to provide concrete, verifiable information on the extent, frequency, or geographical spread of use, and nor does it show the mark’s function as an indicator of commercial origin for goods. In addition, while the evidence contains information, albeit scarce, concerning the possible commercialization of candles, any information is missing regarding some of the remaining goods invoked, namely illuminating wax; lighting apparatus and installations.

In the absence of objective and independent commercial documentation demonstrating significant use of the mark on the relevant market, the requirement of use of more than mere local significance is not fulfilled under EUIPO practice.

Considering all the above, the Opposition Division concludes that the evidence submitted by the opponent is insufficient to prove that the earlier sign was used in the course of trade of more than local significance in connection with the goods on which the opposition was based before the relevant date and in the relevant territory.

As one of the necessary requirements of Article 8(4) EUTMR is not met, the opposition must be rejected as unfounded.

COSTS

According to Article 109(1) EUTMR, the losing party in opposition proceedings must bear the fees and costs incurred by the other party.

Since the opponent is the losing party, it must bear the costs incurred by the applicant in the course of these proceedings.

According to Article 109(7) EUTMR and Article 18(1)(c)(i) EUTMIR, the costs to be paid to the applicant are the costs of representation, which are to be fixed on the basis of the maximum rate set therein.

The Opposition Division

According to Article 67 EUTMR, any party adversely affected by this decision has a right to appeal against this decision. According to Article 68 EUTMR, notice of appeal must be filed in writing at the Office within two months of the date of notification of this decision. It must be filed in the language of the proceedings in which the decision subject to appeal was taken. Furthermore, a written statement of the grounds for appeal must be filed within four months of the same date. The notice of appeal will be deemed to have been filed only when the appeal fee of EUR 720 has been paid.
